skills: Year 1
One language properly: write the language CSE 103 teaches without looking things up, then carry it into objects in CSE 110.
Git every day: commit, branch, push. A GitHub profile with your lab work on it.
The terminal, a real editor and touch typing.
100 solved problems on an online judge before CSE 207.
Year 2
Data structures and algorithms until you can explain the trade-offs out loud (CSE 207, CSE 246).
SQL and schema design from CSE 302 - on a database you designed, not the lab's.
Linux as your daily system for at least one semester (it pays back in CSE 325).
One web or mobile stack, taken to a deployed project.
Year 3
A team project with pull requests and code review (CSE 347 is a natural home).
Networks you can see: packet captures and a socket program alongside CSE 405.
The toolchain of your major: a Python data stack, a testing framework, a network simulator, or an HDL and an FPGA board.
Reading one research paper a month in a department research area.
Year 4
A capstone you can demo in three minutes and defend for thirty.
System-design basics and interview practice: two timed problems a week.
An internship, an open-source contribution or a contest ranking - one outside proof.
A one-page CV, a clean GitHub and a LinkedIn profile that all tell the same story.
dept.career_intro: A CSE degree opens more doors than any one student can walk through, so pick a direction by your third year and let your major, electives and capstone point the same way. These are the common directions; none of them is an EWU rule.
careers: Software engineering
Building and maintaining web, mobile and backend systems in product companies and software houses.
Two finished projects, Git history, data structures and algorithms practice.
Data and machine learning
Cleaning data, building models and putting them into products.
Statistics, Python, one end-to-end project with real data; the Intelligent Systems and Data Science major.
Quality assurance and testing
Designing tests, automating them and guarding releases.
The Software Engineering major's testing course, one automation framework.
Networks, cloud and DevOps
Running the infrastructure that software lives on.
Linux, networking labs, a cloud free-tier project; the Communications and Networking major.
Cyber security
Finding and closing weaknesses in systems and networks.
Networks first, then security labs and capture-the-flag practice; the Cyber Security Club.
Embedded systems and IoT
Software that runs on hardware: devices, sensors, controllers.
Digital logic, microcontrollers, a working device; the Hardware Engineering major and the Robotics Club.
Research and higher study
A master's or PhD, then research or teaching.
CGPA, a research-flavoured capstone, a paper or poster, two recommenders who know your work.
Banks and the public sector
IT officer and programmer roles filled through recruitment examinations.
Core theory kept fresh (DBMS, OS, networks, algorithms) plus the general sections those exams carry.

book.title: The CSE Degree Planner
book.subtitle: Department of Computer Science & Engineering, East West University
lines: Every course, every prerequisite and every capstone milestone of your CSE degree on one map - with the CGPA math done for you.
small: Curriculum, rules, fees and dates checked against East West University's official web pages on 10 October 2026.

Unofficial. An independent planner for students. Not affiliated with, endorsed by or issued by East West University. Always confirm requirements with your advisor, the student portal and official notices.

book.text: Read this first

This planner puts your whole CSE degree in one place: every published course, the rules that move your CGPA, the dates that cost money, and a working page for every week of the semester - on your phone, offline, with the arithmetic done for you.
What you are holding

items: **Degree** - the B.Sc. in Computer Science and Engineering and B.Sc. in Information and Communication Engineering as EWU prints it: every course, its credits and its prerequisite. Pick a semester and a grade per course and the CGPA, the credit map, the Ready / Locked checks and your semester-by-semester plan follow.
**CGPA** - the grading scale, a quick semester GPA, what it takes to reach a target, a retake what-if on EWU's own rule, and the CGPA lines that decide waivers and standing.
**Money** - this semester's bill at the published rates, the whole degree roughly, and the dates that cost money with a countdown you can send to your calendar.
**Semester** - deadlines and tasks, your routine with a clash check, and the working pages of a semester (set-up, course pages, check-ins, finals plan), one set per semester.
**Toolkit** - the tools this department's work actually needs, with logs and calculators that count and flag as you type.
**Rules** - EWU's own grading, retake, probation, load, scholarship and fee rules, with the source named under each.
**More** - clubs and careers, the printable pages, an assignment cover page, the Excel version of the tracker, and your backup.

book.text: What it is not

items: It is **not an official EWU document**. Nobody at the university wrote, checked or approved it.
It does **not replace your advisor**, your advising sheet or the student portal. Those decide what counts toward your degree.

It is **a snapshot**. Course lists, fees, CGPA lines and dates were read from EWU's own web pages on 10 October 2026. Universities change these. When a notice and this planner disagree - cross the old line out here, and the notice wins.

book.text: Start in 15 minutes

items: On **Home**, type your name, the semester you were admitted in and the semester you are in now.
On **Degree**, pick the semester and the grade of every course you have passed. Your CGPA appears at once, and every course shows Ready, Locked or Open.
On **Money**, type this semester's fee and drop dates from the Registrar's calendar; they count down on Home.
On **Semester**, put your sections into the routine and your deadlines into the task list.
Open the **Toolkit** when the work starts: labs, projects, cases, the final-year runway.

book.text: Your data

Everything you type stays in this browser on this device - nothing is sent anywhere, there is no account and no internet is needed. That also means a cleared browser or a new phone starts empty. So, now and then, open **More** and tap **Save this planner with my data inside**: you get this same file back with everything you have typed written into it. Keep that copy - open it on a laptop, send it to a new phone, or hand it to next semester's you.

If a browser refuses to keep your data between visits (some phones open files in a way that forgets), Home tells you so and offers the same button. Your planner is then simply the latest copy you saved.

the Rules tab - Rules that move your CGPA and your money

Most students learn these rules by breaking one. Read them once now. Everything here is taken from East West University's published pages as they stood on 10 October 2026; the source is named under each section.
The grading scale
A+ to D are passing grades. F is failing: it earns no credit and counts as zero in your GPA.
How your GPA and CGPA are worked out

Every course gives you **quality points = credits x grade point**. Add the quality points for a semester and divide by the credits you attempted for a letter grade: that is your semester GPA. Do the same across all semesters and you have your CGPA.
Three things students get wrong

items: **An F stays in the sum.** It adds credits to the bottom of the fraction and nothing to the top, until you retake the course and the old F becomes an R.
**Heavier courses move the CGPA more.** A 4-credit course with a lab outweighs a 3-credit one. Protect the heavy courses first.
**W, I, P and S never enter the GPA.** A W costs you the fee and the semester's work, not grade points.

book.text: Codes that are not letter grades

rows: Incomplete. Given only at the end of a semester when everything except the final exam is done; the instructor files an Incomplete Grade Form.
Finish within one week of the next semester's start (the calendar prints the 'last day to clear I grades'). After that it turns into an F, or into the tentative grade if one was assigned.
Withdrawal. You officially dropped the course before the calendar's withdrawal deadline. No credit, not in GPA.
Use it on purpose, not by accident: the deadline falls about two weeks before classes end.
A repeated course. An earlier attempt that a retake has replaced. No credit, not in GPA, still printed on the grade report.
Pass / Satisfactory. Counts toward graduation, not in GPA.

book.text: Source: EWU 'Grades, Rules and Regulations' page, ewubd.edu/grades-rules-and-regulations.
Retakes

items: You may retake a course **only once** to improve a grade you already earned.
An **F can be retaken as many times as it takes** to pass, inside the time limit for graduation. The earlier F becomes R.
Only your **most recent attempt** counts in GPA and CGPA. Every attempt stays on the grade report.
A retake needs the **Department Chair's written permission** and full tuition, lab and other fees.
Students who use the retake policy are **not eligible for the Gold Medal, awards or distinction**, and the scholarship rules list retaking courses among the things that make a student ineligible.

book.title: Before you retake a passing grade
items: Run the numbers in the CGPA tab's retake what-if. A B- to A- retake on a 3-credit course lifts 2.25 quality points - on 90 GPA credits that is 0.025 of CGPA. Decide whether that is worth a full course fee and your scholarship eligibility.

book.text: Standing, probation and leave

rows: CGPA from 1.00 to below 2.25 after your first two semesters, or any later one, puts you on probation for the next two semesters. Reach 2.25 by then or be dismissed. On probation you cannot drop a semester or take leave.
CGPA below 1.00 after the first two or any later semester means automatic dismissal. A dismissed student may apply to another program by passing its admission test.
The academic calendar sets an in-person advising day for students with CGPA 2.15 or less (admitted up to Summer 2023) or 2.40 or less (admitted from Fall 2023), and for everyone on probation.

A student in good standing can take up to three consecutive semesters (one academic year) of leave through the Dean, naming the return semester. Absence without permission is penalised - 20%, 30% or 40% of nine credits' tuition for one, two or three semesters - and beyond three semesters you are withdrawn.
The student rules ask for attendance of not less than 70%-80% of lectures, tutorials and practical classes in each course. Check each course outline for the figure your instructor applies.

Final scripts are not re-evaluated. You can ask for a check of marking or totalling errors for Tk 200 a script (refunded if the error was the faculty member's). Grade changes must reach the Controller of Examinations within seven days of the next semester.

Zero tolerance for copying, unauthorised help and other unfair means; cases go to the Dean. EWU also publishes a Plagiarism Policy and an Artificial Intelligence Policy (ewubd.edu/ewu-policies) - read both before you submit work made with any tool.

book.text: the Toolkit tab - The CSE toolkit
Seven tools for the work this department actually sets: choosing a major, surviving lab-heavy courses, building things worth showing, and landing the capstone.
1. Choose your major on purpose

The B.Sc. in CSE asks you to pick **one of four major areas** and take its 2 compulsory courses and 3 of its electives (20 credits), then at least 8 credits of non-major electives from other areas. The compulsory courses have their own prerequisites, so the choice starts earlier than it looks.

rows: you enjoy statistics, patterns in data and making models behave.
CSE 430 Software Testing and Quality Assurance
you like building complete products with a team and getting the details right.
you want to know how bits move: signals, protocols, wireless and security.
you like logic, circuits and code that makes a physical thing work.

book.text: Score each area from 1 to 5. Decide by the end of Year 2 so that Year 3's two compulsory major slots are ready to fill.
ICE students: the department website does not publish the ICE course list. Use the blank degree map in the Degree tab and ask your advisor which elective areas apply to you.
2. Capstone runway (CSE 400)

CSE 400 Capstone Project is **6 credits**, needs **at least 105 completed credit hours**, and the department's flowchart runs it across the three semesters of Year 4 as Capstone I (1 credit), II (2 credits) and III (3 credits). Start the runway a semester earlier than that.

rows: A team that has worked together once. Three problem ideas, each written as one paragraph. A shortlist of supervisors whose research areas match.
Supervisor confirmed. Problem statement, objectives and scope agreed in writing. Survey of existing systems or papers. Requirements and a risk list. Repository and task board set up.
Design signed off. A working core: the hardest part of the system running end to end, even if ugly. Test plan. Mid-way presentation.
Feature-complete build, tested with real users or real data. Results measured against the objectives. Report, poster or paper, demo video, final defence.

book.text: 3. The lab-course loop
Courses with a lab component (CSE 103, 110, 207, 246, 302 and most of what follows) are won in the hours around the lab, not in it. Run the same loop every week.

rows: Read the task sheet. Write the approach in plain sentences or pseudo-code. List what you do not know yet and look up exactly that.
Get the simplest version working first. Commit when it runs. Ask the question you wrote down. Note what the instructor checks during evaluation.
Rewrite the solution cleanly without looking at the lab version. Add the edge cases. Push to your repository with a two-line README.
Do one extra problem on the same idea from an online judge or the textbook.

book.text: Bug journal

Lab report and viva checklist

items: Title, course code, experiment number, date, my name and ID are on the first page.
The objective is one or two sentences in my own words.
Code is formatted, commented where it is not obvious, and matches what I ran.
Every output is labelled; screenshots are readable; circuit diagrams and truth tables are drawn, not photographed sideways.
The discussion says what happened, why, and what I would change - not a repeat of the procedure.
I can explain any line or component if asked in the viva, and I know the complexity or the timing of what I built.
Submitted in the format and by the time the lab instructor set.

book.text: 4. Problem-solving log
Contest practice is the cheapest way to make CSE 207 and CSE 246 easy and interviews boring. Climb the ladder in order; log every problem, including the ones you could not solve.
